title: Columba of Iona (563)
hookLine: an Irish monk exiles himself to an island and sends missions to Scotland

cards: A white horse, the one that carries the milk pails, walks up to a tired man resting by the road on a small island. It lays its head on his chest and, in the story, begins to weep. His servant moves to drive it away.
The old man stops him. Let it be, he says; it loves me, and it knows I'm leaving. That man is Columba, an Irish monk, and the island is Iona, off the coast of what's now Scotland.
He came there by choice, and it was there he died.

teach.b: Our source is Adomnán, a later abbot of Iona, who wrote Columba's life from what the community remembered.
He gives Columba's reason for leaving Ireland in a single phrase: he sailed away wishing to be a pilgrim for Christ.
Not someone who goes to a holy place and comes back, but someone who leaves home for good, for God's sake, and lives as a stranger.
A later story says he left as a penance, after a quarrel that ended in a battle; Adomnán gives no such reason.
On Iona, Columba built a monastery. Monks prayed, farmed, fished, studied, and copied scripture, and Adomnán shows Columba himself at a writing desk. From that small island, monks went out.
Adomnán tells of Columba traveling to the fortress of Bridei, a king of the Picts.

teach.h: THE GATES OF THE PICTISH KING.
teach.b: The king shut his gates against him. Columba made the sign of the cross on the doors, knocked, and, in Adomnán's telling, the bolts drew back on their own, and the king came out to meet him with respect.
Now the end. In his last days, Adomnán says, Columba was copying the psalms in his hut. He reached a verse saying that those who seek the Lord shall not lack any good thing, and stopped there.

Let the next part be written by the one who comes after me, he said, meaning his successor. That night he went to the church for the midnight prayer and died before the altar, surrounded by his monks.
Catholics honor him as a saint, and Iona is still a place of pilgrimage.
An island at the edge of the map became, for a time, a center that sent people out.

how: Catholics in Ireland and Scotland keep the feast of Saint Columba, also called Colmcille, and pilgrims still travel to Iona.

o: Latin for a monk who copies scripture
Latin for an exile sent away as a penance
Latin for a pilgrim, a stranger for Christ

games.q: Columba of Iona — tap the pairs.

s: Adomnán says Columba left Ireland as a penance for a battle
that's a later story; Adomnán says he went wishing to be a pilgrim for Christ.
in Adomnán's telling, the Pictish king's gates opened after Columba made the sign of the cross
the bolts drew back and the king came out to meet him.
Columba finished copying the whole psalter before he died
he stopped at a verse about those who seek the Lord and left the rest to his successor.

games.q: you're Columba at the gates of a king who has shut them against you. what do you do?
o: go home and try another kingdom.
make the sign of the cross on the doors and knock.
wait outside until the king gets curious.
games.why: Adomnán says Columba signed the doors with the cross and knocked, and the bolts drew back on their own.

practice: Columba left his homeland and spent his life sending good news into another; bring your own country's people to mind, not its news: a town you know, neighbors, someone going to bed hungry tonight, someone who governs.
If you pray, pray for them by name or in silence; if you don't, simply wish them well.

wordCard.voice: peregrinus. Latin for a pilgrim or stranger, what Columba wanted to be for Christ when he sailed away from Ireland to Iona. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a pilgrim or stranger — what Adomnán says Columba wanted to be for Christ.

carryVoice: Your line: the island. Wherever you live, that place is worth your prayers too. See you tomorrow.
